title: 'Fake News' in urology: evaluating the accuracy of articles shared on social media in genitourinary malignancies
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 10 most-shared social-media articles for each of five genitourinary-malignancy topics (50 articles, Buzzsumo, Aug 2017-Aug 2018). Two physicians independently classified each article accurate / inaccurate / misleading against the scientific literature and consensus data (kappa = 0.91): 15/50 (30%) were inaccurate or misleading. A quantitative share of items judged against external ground truth, with an explicit denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language articles identified worldwide via Buzzsumo (authors US-based, Loma Linda University)
estimates.platform: Articles shared on Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit (shares pooled across platforms)
estimates.date: Articles identified between August 2017 and August 2018
estimates.measure_type: % of the 50 most-shared social-media articles on genitourinary malignancies classified as inaccurate or misleading
estimates.value_raw: 15/50 articles (30%) inaccurate or misleading; 35/50 articles (70%) accurate
estimates.denominator: 50 articles: the 10 most-shared English-language articles on each of prostate cancer, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, testis cancer and PSA testing, identified with Buzzsumo across Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit
estimates.definition: 'Articles were classified as inaccurate if they contained information that is not supported or has been refuted by scientific literature or consensus data. Articles were classified as misleading if they contained both accurate and inaccurate information or if they discussed prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of a malignancy based on animal research studies with no supporting evidence in human subject research.' The numerator combines both categories.
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper uses '“Fake News”' and 'misinformation' without a formal definition; operationally 'inaccurate' = 'information that is not supported or has been refuted by scientific literature or consensus data'
estimates.source_quote: A total of 35/50 articles (70%) were classified as accurate; only 40.0% (14/35) of the accurate articles were affiliated with an official institutional website, while 8.6% (3/35) were shared directly from a peer-reviewed journal website. The remaining articles (51.4%) were shared from non-affiliated and non-peer reviewed websites. A total of 15/50 articles (30%) were classified as inaccurate or misleading
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 'A total of 50 articles were reviewed for accuracy independently by two physicians. The article information was compared against available scientific research and consensus data using the databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Sciences and Google Scholar.' Discordance was resolved by the principal investigator, blinded to the reviewers' decisions. Inter-rater agreement reported: Cohen's kappa = 0.91 (CI 0.80-1.00), 'almost perfect'.
estimates.moderator_quote: The top 10 shared articles for each malignancy topic were selected for analysis as articles with lower rankings had a significantly lower number of shares and were therefore considered low-impact articles (articles with less than 100 shares were considered low-impact).
estimates.notes: Denominator is items that exist in a rank-truncated (top-10 per topic) multi-topic keyword corpus, hence denom_scope=topical + denom_selection=curated. Coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY: the judgement is explicit accurate/inaccurate coding against the scientific literature. FLAG FOR ADJUDICATOR: one limb of the 'misleading' definition - discussing prevention/diagnosis/treatment based on animal research 'with no supporting evidence in human subject research' - could in principle attach to a factually correct article; Table 1 shows this limb accounts for only 2 of the 15 flagged articles, so the row is kept as CONTENT rather than QUALITY. Topic coded health_other (urological cancers), not covid19.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Per-malignancy splits are verbatim but were not written as rows: inaccurate-or-misleading prostate cancer 7/10, kidney cancer 3/10, bladder cancer 2/10, testis cancer 2/10, PSA testing 1/10 (Figure 2); inaccurate-only prostate 4/10, kidney 2/10, bladder 1/10, testis 1/10, PSA 0/10. Reason: these are sub-topics of one health domain (all would code topic=health_other, same country, same platform set), each cell has n=10, and the pooled row already carries the information. An adjudicator wanting a strict-falsity variant would have to sum 4+2+1+1+0 = 8/50 (16%), which is a cross-category sum forbidden by R8 - the paper never prints a pooled inaccurate-only figure. 2) No SHARING row is derivable: average shares are reported by accuracy class (inaccurate 54,000; misleading 7,040; accurate 1,900) and per platform (Facebook 9,051; Twitter 5,320; Reddit 2,081; Pinterest 248), but these are means, not shares of total shares, and computing 482,380/547,766 from Table 1 plus Figure 1 would require two cross-category sums (forbidden). 'Inaccurate articles were 28 times more likely to be shared than accurate articles' is a ratio of means, not a proportion. 3) Provenance shares (14/35 = 40.0% of accurate articles from official institutional websites; 3/35 = 8.6% from peer-reviewed journal websites; 51.4% from non-affiliated/non-peer-reviewed sites) are source-type shares within the accurate subset, not veracity shares, so no row. 4) '69% of adult internet users are active on social media platforms' and '74% of urologists reported having an online social media account' are cited from other sources - excluded under R8. 5) No survey, exposure, reach or concentration data.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated web corpus. Frame: Buzzsumo keyword searches for prostate cancer, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, testis cancer and PSA testing across Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit, August 2017-August 2018; the 10 most-shared English-language articles per topic were retained (n = 50); articles with expired links were excluded; identical articles republished on different websites were merged into one. No probability sampling and no response rate. Coding: two physicians independently classified every article as accurate, inaccurate or misleading against PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar evidence and consensus data; discordance was resolved by the principal investigator blinded to the reviewers' decisions. Reliability reported: Cohen's kappa = 0.91 (95% CI 0.80-1.00). Mann-Whitney U tests for share comparisons. Author-stated limitations: only the most-shared articles on selected diagnostic search terms (no symptom-based terms), inability to tell endorsing from critical shares, and a proprietary Buzzsumo algorithm that could not be validated.
